text: 3.1 Existing Methods
Elections today are run in three main ways, each with strengths and weaknesses.

items: **Paper ballots.** Trust comes from physical observation. They are transparent to those present at the booth and the count, but are slow, costly, hard for absent voters and open to local tampering such as booth capturing.
**Electronic voting machines.** They are fast and widely used, but voters and observers cannot inspect the software inside, and an independent recount is limited to the machine's own record.
**Online voting through a central server.** It is convenient, but the server operator can in principle change or read votes, and a single attack on the server can affect the whole election.

**Earlier blockchain prototypes.** They remove the central record keeper but, as shown in Section 1.1, often leave identity linked to the vote, give one party the decryption key, or enforce rules in the web server.

text: 3.2 Proposed Method
The proposed system divides the trust. No single component or person is able to break the secrecy or the integrity of the election alone.

items: The **backend** knows who is eligible and who has voted, but it sees only an encrypted ballot and a random token. It cannot read a vote.
The **blockchain contract** holds the encrypted ballots and enforces the rules. It cannot read a vote either, and it knows nothing about the voters' identities.
The **trustees** can decrypt, but only together (two of three), and only after the election has closed.
The **public** can verify everything: the ballots on the chain, the published key and the tally.

text: Two ideas keep the identity and the ballot apart. First, the voter is known to the backend only by a hash, the Keccak-256 of an HMAC of the voter's identity token, so the electoral roll does not contain raw identities. Second, when the voter is verified the backend issues a random single-use token. The database stores only the hash of the token, and the table that holds tokens has no voter column and no timestamp, so a token cannot be linked to the person it was given to, even by someone who reads the whole database.
3.3 System Overview, Block Diagram and Flow Chart

Figure 3.1 shows the block diagram of the system. The voter's browser performs the encryption. The backend, a Node.js server, handles registration, OTP authentication, voter verification, token issue and submission of ballots. The smart contract on the Ethereum blockchain stores the ballots and the result. The trustees use their own command-line tools, away from the server.

text: 3.4 Main Components
3.4.1 Registration and OTP authentication

A voter enters an identity number and requests an OTP. A mock service, which stands in for the UIDAI Aadhaar OTP service, generates a six-digit code that is valid for five minutes and allows three attempts. After a correct OTP the voter receives a session that lasts ten minutes. Requests are rate-limited, and the server writes no access log so that it keeps no record of who connected when.
3.4.2 Voter verification and single-use token

The voter hash is calculated as Keccak-256(HMAC-SHA-256(secret, "voter:" + identity token)). The HMAC with a server secret stops anyone from guessing identities by hashing every possible number. The backend checks the hash against the electoral roll and, if the voter is eligible and has not yet received a token, issues a token of 32 random bytes. Only the Keccak-256 hash of the token is stored. The voter's record is only flagged as token issued, so a second token is refused.
3.4.3 Ballot encryption

The browser encrypts the ballot using the Web Crypto interface. The plaintext is 17 bytes: one byte for the candidate number and 16 random bytes, which make two votes for the same candidate look completely different. The plaintext is encrypted with a fresh AES-256 key in Galois/Counter Mode, and that AES key is wrapped with the election's RSA-3072 public key using OAEP with SHA-256. The associated data "gov-evoting:v1:<chain id>:<contract address>" is authenticated with the ciphertext, so a ballot cannot be moved to a different election. The result is always 430 bytes (Figure 3.4), whichever candidate is chosen, so the size of a ballot reveals nothing.

caption: Figure 3.4: Structure of an encrypted ballot (430 bytes)

text: 3.4.4 Smart contract (GovElection)
The Solidity contract keeps the election. Its main rules are given below.

items: Phases: Setup, Voting, Closed and Finalized, moving forward only.

Only the backend's submitter account can call castBallot(tokenHash, ballot). Each token hash can be used once, a ballot may be at most 1,024 bytes, and the number of ballots cannot exceed the number of eligible voters.
The hash of the election key is stored when the contract is created and cannot be changed.
After the end time, anyone can call closeElection(); nobody can close it early.
Trustees call submitTally(); the result is finalised only when two trustees submit identical totals.
Every important step emits an event, so the full history is public.

text: 3.4.5 Key ceremony and trustees

Before the election a key ceremony generates the RSA-3072 key pair. The private key is split by Shamir secret sharing into three shares, any two of which rebuild it. Each share is encrypted for its trustee with a passphrase of at least twelve characters, using scrypt (N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1) to derive the key and AES-256-GCM to protect the share, with the share's details bound in as authenticated data. Only the hash of the public key is placed in the contract, and the plain private key is never saved to disk.
3.4.6 Tally and public verification

After the election closes, two trustees supply their shares and passphrases, the private key is rebuilt, and its hash is compared with the hash stored on the chain. Each ballot is decrypted; a ballot that cannot be decrypted, or that names a candidate who does not exist, is counted as invalid and never stops the count. The trustees submit the totals together with a tally hash. When two identical submissions arrive the contract finalises the result. The private key is then published, and the verify-tally tool lets anyone download the ballots from the chain, decrypt them and check that the totals match.
3.5 Workflow of the System

items: **Setup.** The administrator runs the key ceremony, and the contract is deployed with the candidates, the trustees, the submitter, the voter limit and the hash of the election key.
**Registration.** Voters are placed on the electoral roll as voter hashes.
**Opening.** The administrator opens the election for a fixed time window.
**Login.** The voter requests and enters the OTP and receives a session.
**Verification and token.** The backend checks the voter hash, then issues the one-time token.
**Voting.** The browser encrypts the ballot; the backend submits it to the contract with the token hash; the voter sees a receipt.
**Closing.** When the end time passes, anyone can close the election.
**Tally.** Two trustees rebuild the key, decrypt, and submit identical totals; the contract finalises the result.
**Verification.** The key is published, and anyone can recount.

text: 3.6 Design Constraints

caption: Table 3.1: Design constraints and how they were handled
rows: Voter known only by a keyed hash; token table has no voter column or timestamp; fixed-size ballots; no access log.
Rules enforced by the smart contract; ballots permanent on the chain; key hash fixed at deployment.
OTP login and electoral roll check; one token per voter; one ballot per token.
2-of-3 threshold for decryption and for the tally.
Ballot kept at 430 bytes; about 417,000 gas per vote (Section 5.1).
Whole pipeline about 0.23 s per vote on a laptop.
One-button voting page; no wallet or crypto knowledge needed by the voter.
Raw identity numbers are not stored; the identity service is simulated in this prototype.
Transaction queue on the backend; chain reads cached for 3 seconds; limits on request rate.
Free tools only; local test chain; free test network and free cloud tier for deployment.

caption: Table 3.2: Standards and guidelines followed
rows: AES-GCM authenticated encryption of the ballot and of the key shares
RSA-OAEP wrapping of the AES key
SHA-256 inside the HMAC and the key hash; Keccak-256 (the SHA-3 family) for voter and token hashes
Threshold splitting of the election private key
Input validation, rate limiting, safe error messages, no secrets in logs
Strict policy on the web pages to limit script injection
Minimal personal data; identity not stored in raw form
